Name: Noah Luken
Q1: I believe that effective governance on campus should enhance student life significantly. Unfortunately, I do not feel confident saying that student life has improved as much as it could have since I've been a student here. I want to be the change that I would like to see on campus, and for that reason, I am running to be a Senator with the 76th Senate. From day one, I want to ensure that the Senate is fulfilling its role as a policymaking body that supports students and doesn't get bogged down in political drama.
Q2: This year, I began working in the A.S. Attorney General's Office as a research assistant and caseworker. As a result, I've developed a strong understanding of legal code, even writing resolutions that I presented to and were voted on by the Senate. As a first-year, I was a floor representative for my hall council in San Miguel. This gave me a taste of what it's like to serve on behalf of my peers. Since my first-year, I've been an editor for the UCSB Undergraduate Law Journal. This has engrained in me the importance of the little details, something that is critical when considering how a bill or resolution will affect the campus and A.S. finances for years to come. I've also helped found an organization that will likely be a RCO by the fall called Gaucho Think Tank. We hope to write policy and implement solutions with the help of art/outreach in a collaboration between writers, scientists, engineers, artists, thinkers, and all other members of the campus community.
Q3:
1. Fee Transparency Act - An act that would allow detailed breakdowns of what student fees are used for to be easily accessible on BARC statements. 
2. Legal Code Examination Act - An act that would clean up the ridiculously long, inaccessible, and repetitive legal code. 
3. Student Aid Act - An act that would, in collaboration with administration, provide an easy route towards aid for textbooks and online software like ALEKS that cause financial burden for many students. 
4. Leadership Accessibility Act - An act that would mandate office hours and outreach in some capacity by Senators and execs to ensure more transparency and accountability with the student body. It would also create (at a minimum) quarterly town halls for the Senate to respond to student concerns.
Q4:
Student government shouldn’t be an exclusive club for budget approvals and closed-door meetings—it should be a tool for real change. Too often, A.S. quietly passes resolutions that don’t directly benefit students.

For example, the Senate this year passed a resolution to “affirm their strong support” for “enduring dining hall reform.” Instead of allocating money or creating a program to help, the Senate thought the best they could do was to send their best wishes to those actually doing the hard, important work.

It's a shame that student fees every quarter aren’t put to optimal use. While the current Senate uses their super-duper strong words, here’s what I want to concretely fix:
1. TRANSPARENCY FOR STUDENT FEES – You pay them, you should know where they go. No more hoping the “U/G Campus Fee” and “Stdt Services Fee” on your BARC statements ($1,000+ per quarter) are being put to good use without knowing exactly how your money is being spent. I'll push for clear, accessible breakdowns so we can hold A.S. leaders and administration accountable.
2. REAL SUPPORT FOR FOOD & HOUSING INSECURITY – No student should be picking between an online textbook and groceries. I’ll fight for expanded meal-share programs, emergency housing support, and stronger financial aid advocacy.
3. BREAKING DOWN BARRIERS TO STUDENT GOVERNMENT – A.S. should serve you, not be a closed-door club. I’ll push for better outreach so you know what A.S. is doing and how it can improve your student experience.

I’m not here to build a resume—I’m here to make sure A.S. works for you.
Q5: Most importantly, I hope to be accessible to any and all organizations or entities. My platform is the students of UCSB. That is to say, my goals are the students' goals. I want to shape my time in Senate around fulfilling the needs and wants of A.S. members. In terms of specific organizations, I have an affinity for sustainability groups like Gauchos Go Green. I always believe there are ways to improve sustainability practices in the community. Furthermore, I hope to engage with the work that BCUs like the Commission on Student Well Being and the A.S. Bike Shop to complete projects that positively impact students.
Q6: I will hold weekly office hours, and I intend to publicize myself as a sort of liaison between the student body and the rest of A.S. I'm sick and tired of students not knowing what A.S. does because leaders haven't done a good enough job of showing them. It pains me that so many individuals have ideas, but most of the time they are never heard because they don't know where to bring them. Furthermore, I intend to create a town hall system for the Senate where constituents can come and engage with A.S. leaders directly.
Q7: My love for UCSB has led to a strong desire to give back. I am the best candidate for this position because I am not interested in boosting my resume, satisfying my ego, or searching for power. Rather, I have a genuine interest in the wellbeing of my peers at school, and I want to do whatever I can to support them. If I can make everyone's time at UCSB just a little bit better, I will consider my term to be a success. I have no regard for any personal gain I may accrue from being a Senator.
Q10: I am looking for the new chancellor of UCSB to have the students' interests at the forefront of their work. Just as we see within the Association, administrators too often get bogged down in the politics of their roles and forget what they should be working towards in the first place. I will ensure regular communication between the new Chancellor and Senate, and I hope that they are responsive to A.S. and student needs.
Q11a: Education is incredibly important to a well-functioning society. Anytime a service such as education can be provided for free, it should be.
Q12: While I love and appreciate the work that mental health services at UCSB like CAPS provide, I believe they must be bolstered in order to better serve students. Too often I hear stories where students are unable to schedule appointments for months and can't find access to the resources they need. To address the issue, A.S. leaders need to cooperate with administration to best understand what students feel they need and are missing. Then, action must be taken by the same parties to rectify the observed systemic faults.
Q13: I am familiar with the university's Title IX office and its functions. To support survivors, the university needs to ensure free access to professionals who can help survivors with whatever they need or want. Furthermore, well-oiled systems must be in place that ensure particular responses from the university whenever instances of sexual violence are reported.
Q14: While I appreciate the wonderful work that organizations representing historically underrepresented groups do on our campus and in Isla Vista, I am certain that there is more the university can do to ensure that everyone's needs are met. Particularly, UCSB should focus on fostering dialogue between these groups, A.S., and administration to help with the sharing of perspectives that leads to positive change. I will continue to be an ally to and supporter of such groups as long as I am alive.
Q15: As written, I will hold weekly office hours, regularly communicate with various groups on campus, and focus on creating avenues for dialogue between A.S. leaders and students from all walks of life. This will not only allow for students' ideas to be shared with A.S. leaders, but it will provide spaces for leaders to share with fellow students what is being done by A.S. on their behalf. There is a lot of good work that A.S. does every year, and it is important that members know these things so that the positive aspects can be fully enjoyed.
Q16: I intend to work in close collaboration with administration to guarantee that we as a community are doing everything in our power to protect international students as they are highly valued members of the community. Furthermore, I hope to solidify policies at the campus and UC levels that provide protections for students that find themselves victim to such terrible circumstances. Additionally, I would like to create anonymous tip channels where concerned students can speak confidentially with legal professionals, for example.
Q17: Collaboration is the key to success. As an extroverted individual, I hope to work with and take into account the ideas of others as I strive to make campus a better place. I want to usher in an era of positive governance, free from the ills of political gaming that has plagued the current Senate. In doing so, I am certain that we will be able to accomplish not only material success, but cultivate a climate of enduring positivity across campus.

Name: Evan Sussman
Q1:
Our student government should be more representative of pressing issues facing our students, and I want to make students’ experiences at UCSB the best they can be.
I have been a leader in student government since elementary school. I was president of my high school, actively involved with the YMCA’s youth and government, and a person who aspires to be a leader. Coming into UCSB, I knew I wanted to be involved with A.S. As I progressed through my freshman year, like most students here, I simply did not know how to navigate our student government. I felt so disconnected from the very program that should represent and be accessible to ALL students. Fortunately, I was accepted as a Pearman Fellow this year; however, while observing different offices within A.S., I noticed a clear and present disconnect between the branches, and, most importantly, a disconnect with the student body. I know how student government works, and I know how to communicate and lead effectively. Currently, AS lacks these two critical aspects. Students do not feel like the current AS is representative of the most important student concerns, and is prioritizing other concerns. When I tell my friends that AS has a budget of $16 million, the response has been a mix of utter confusion and anger, and I, for one, cannot blame them. I am running because I am passionate about helping others. My dream is to go into government, but my current goal is to enhance the student experience here at UCSB.
Q2: Throughout my first year at UCSB, I had the honor of being a Pearman Fellow in the office of the External Vice President of State Affairs (EVPSA). Through this fellowship, I worked closely with the legislative division, analyzing California and federal legislation that impacts higher education. Furthermore, I am a Lobby Corps delegate, which is a BCU that is funded by AS, and I went to the State Capitol in Sacramento to lobby on statewide higher education initiatives. Likewise, I am involved with the Student Homes Coalition, which focuses on improving housing accessibility across California, and will be lobbying next month to increase student and resident housing options throughout the state. At the same time, I often observe senate meetings, proxy for current senators, and gain relevant experience within AS. I am also a student worker, so I understand the importance of paying student fees and tuition. I serve as the Director of Engagement and Outreach for UCSB First, a philanthropy group on campus, which has provided me with the tools and assets necessary to work and collaborate with various groups and organizations on campus. With years of leadership experience, writing legislation in youth government, and current legislative analysis of federal and state bills, I understand the role it takes to be a senator. Most importantly, I know the responsibility and commitment I am taking to improve our school.
Q3:
The following bills and legislation that I will introduce aim to make AS more efficient, which in turn benefits our student body. I also plan to introduce additional ideas during my term, such as increasing support for the AS Food Bank and launching a special project to revitalize the UCEN. But these are my top three priorities:
1) AS Transparency Initiative: One of the most frustrating aspects of AS that I’ve noticed is the lack of communication within AS itself. If our own elected officials don’t even know what the other is doing, how can we expect students to feel involved or informed? Through this initiative, I’ll convene quarterly meetings with representatives from every AS branch; Office of the President, EVPSA, EVPLA, IVP, Program Board, Attorney General, and Senate; so we can actually sit down, coordinate, set shared goals, and make sure our $16 million budget is being used in a unified, strategic way. We MUST talk to each other. I will push for that all year.
2) BCU Accountability Bill: AS funds all of our BCUs, but sometimes there is no clear record of how the money is being used. This bill would require each BCU to submit quarterly expenditure reports, student engagement updates, and event summaries every quarter. This isn’t about micromanagement—it’s about transparency and helping these groups succeed by providing them with the necessary support.
3) Chancellor’s Housing Commitment Bill: With a new chancellor starting in 2025, we cannot stay silent. From day one, I will push to ensure that San Benito Village is completed by 2027, and I will demand clear timelines for the demolition of Santa Rosa and Ortega and their replacement buildings. I’ll also work with off-campus senators to ensure IV tenants are supported and not taken advantage of by landlords.
Q4:
My platform has 3 main objectives: to get organized, get housed, and get your money's worth. 
GET ORGANIZED: Associated Students can (and should) be more representative of students' wants and needs. With a disconnect between AS and the student body, a more functional, effective, and communicative student government would help us all.  To solve this issue of deep-rooted miscommunication and inefficiency, I will ensure that all branches of our AS communicate efficiently and effectively, prioritizing student needs and wants above all else. 
GET HOUSED: While all first-year students are guaranteed housing, a majority of our students are placed in stressful housing situations following their first year. This is due to the lack of university housing, forcing students to pay extremely high rent rates in Isla Vista. I will hold the university accountable, ensuring it fulfills its commitment to address the housing crisis. This will entail direct collaboration, communication, and pressure on the incoming chancellor's office, as well as continuous efforts from AS as a unified organization. I will further support IV tenants who are being taken advantage of by landlords, and work with my fellow off-campus senators to ensure you have the right resources and information about your tenant rights. 
GET OUR MONEY’S WORTH: As a student worker and someone who is attentive to the tuition and fees of UCSB, I often ask; are we getting what we pay for? We pay for an AS budget of $16 MILLION a year, and I’m not convinced we’re getting the best product. I will utilize our funds in a more fiscally responsible manner to provide a meaningful and purposeful experience at UCSB. This means utilizing the special project fund for campus renovations, ensuring that money is not being wasted on inactive, inefficient, or non-feasible projects and organizations, and, most importantly, ensuring that students understand where their money is going in our AS budget.
Q5:
Much of my platform is grounded in both internal and external collaboration within Associated Students. Internally, I plan to hold all AS offices accountable by initiating quarterly meetings with the Senate to discuss objectives, budgetary decisions, and actionable steps toward our shared goals. I will also oversee the funding, productivity, and student development of BCUs, which will require consistent and transparent communication with BCU leadership.
Externally, I aim to establish a strong working relationship with the incoming Chancellor to advocate for student needs, particularly in areas like housing. I also recognize the important role campus clubs and Greek life play in shaping student experiences. I plan to actively invite all student organizations to collaborate and share how AS can better support the groups that contribute to a vibrant and successful student life, both on and off campus.
Q6:
One of my favorite parts of studying political science and being involved in student government is hearing new perspectives. As a senator, I want to listen, learn, and advocate for you, and I’ll always make myself available. Those who know me know that I’m more than willing to make time, whether it’s a quick check-in or a deeper conversation about policy.
I will maintain consistent office hours and dedicate time before and after Senate meetings to connect with students and discuss policy ideas, bill proposals, or concerns. Whether you want to talk about campus policies, ask questions about the A.S. budget, or grab a coffee and chat, I’m here for you.
I’m committed to serving all students and being as accessible as possible. Please don’t hesitate to reach out. You can contact me via my campaign Instagram account, @sussmanforsenate, or through my personal account, @evan_sussman.
Q7: I am passionate about making change. Since high school, my aspiration in life has been to help people wherever I can. With my past experiences in student government, my leadership knowledge and experience, I can assure all students that I am running to make your student experience the best it can be. I know how student government works; I have been a member of some less-than-ideal student governments, and I have helped lead productive and efficient ones. The results you get from a student government come from the leaders, and I am passionate about leadership. I would say that I am the best candidate for this position because I will represent YOU and YOUR INTERESTS. I am willing to fight for institutional changes within AS to ensure that student interests are truly being represented.
Q10: I am looking for a chancellor who is willing to commit ample time and resources to fixing the housing crisis, and most importantly, a chancellor who will be accountable to their students. Like AS, if the chancellor is not communicating with their students or student representatives, how will the university put student interests first? That is what I aim to fix: to be someone who can communicate with the chancellor's office and make sure that UCSB is fixing the pressing issues facing students.
Q11a: In an ideal world, all college would be free, but the reality is it’s not. However, the administration must do more to make an education at UCSB more affordable
Q12: I believe that the mental health resources are adequate; however, there is always room for improvement. In addition to Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS), which offers excellent resources for group counseling, one-on-one mental health programs, and peer support, several other programs are available to students at UCSB. As someone who has had past struggles with mental health, I understand the importance of and prioritization of providing psychological support. The Disabled Students Program is wonderful for those who face depression or persistent mental health struggles that interfere with education. Accommodations are available for students who require them. While these programs are brilliant and beyond beneficial to UCSB students, AS should advocate and publicize these programs to students who need these resources. Our entire generation of college students has faced extreme challenges to our mental health. The COVID Pandemic affected us all in ways that we are still trying to comprehend. And to be honest, like most people across the world, I too struggled mentally and physically for a long time. If any student is struggling and needs resources or wants to talk, please know that I am here to listen and support you. As a senator, student, and person, I am here for you, and most importantly, YOU GOT THIS!
Q13:
I am familiar with Title IX and how it functions to protect students from discrimination, including sexual harassment and assault. Unfortunately, the reality of college—and of life—is that sexual assault remains a persistent threat to all students. As an Off-Campus Senator, I believe it’s essential to be proactive in prevention, awareness, and survivor support.
As a part of my initiative to work closely with student BCU entities, I will collaborate and communicate with Take Back the Night (TBtN). This student-funded program aims to combat sexual assault, relationship, and domestic violence, and provides survivor support. I will ask for suggestions from TBtN as to legislation I can introduce, as well as what other AS offices can do to take preventative actions and better support students. Everyone deserves to feel safe – on campus, in their homes, and in their communities.
Q14:
I believe UCSB is making a genuine effort to serve historically underrepresented communities, although there is always room for improvement. The university allocates significant time and financial resources to support these groups. For example, the Student Resource Building houses numerous cultural and identity-based centers, including the American Indian and Indigenous Cultural Resource Center and the Middle Eastern, North African, and South Asian Resource Center, among others. For our Latino community, there is El Centro, a community-based safe space on campus where students can find support and resources. For all students, the Multicultural Center (MCC) is available, where they can decompress and connect with peers who share similar or diverse cultural backgrounds. UCSB further supports community-based student clubs, academic departments with diverse initiatives, and identity-based housing.
In addition to university support, Associated Students dedicates substantial financial funding toward these communities, for instance, $111,750 to the Trans & Queer Commission and $45,333.50 to the Black Women's Collaborative, as well as other culture, race, or gender based entities. That said, if these communities feel they are not being adequately served with their budgets, internal evaluations of these programs and their funding must take place. It is essential to assess not only the availability of resources but also their effectiveness in actually meeting students’ needs. Still, from what I’ve seen, UCSB and AS are actively prioritizing support for underrepresented students.
Q15:
I completely agree. A.S. is often seen as a large, inaccessible bureaucracy, and at the root of this issue is poor communication. As of today, the last posted Senate meeting minutes on the A.S. main website date back to 2023. The executive cabinet from TWO YEARS AGO is still listed. This is unacceptable. The Senate Instagram account posts maybe three Canva graphics per quarter, briefly stating which resolutions passed, with no real explanation or context. That’s not transparency—it’s performative.
When I was ASB President in high school, I asked a simple question: How many Canva posts do students actually read? The answer? Almost none.
It’s a disgrace to all UCSB students that we’re working with a $16 million budget, where each senator receives $600+ per quarter, and yet we fail to provide students with even the most basic information about what our government is doing. As a senator, I will work to change that. I will push for weekly video updates posted at both the beginning and end of each week, summarizing key Senate actions, upcoming events, and opportunities to get involved. These videos will provide clear and accessible explanations of passed resolutions and their direct impact on students. I’ll also ensure we publicize opportunities like fellowships, job hirings, and involvement in BCUs across all platforms. I will also commit to publishing Senate agendas and committee updates in a timely and digestible way. 
This isn’t revolutionary. It just requires effort—something the current Senate has too often lacked. When a government doesn’t communicate with its people, it loses their trust. And A.S. is no exception. I’m ready to rebuild that trust by showing up, speaking clearly, and making sure every student knows they have a voice in their student government.
Q16:
While we’re seeing headlines about grant and budget cuts at Ivy League schools, the Trump administration’s education cuts are also impacting our very own university. This has led to budget cuts within our research institutions, including the REEF, and resulted in a direct hiring freeze across the entire UC system. With the future of federal funding for higher education uncertain, research universities like UCSB are stuck in a state of limbo and fear.
As a senator, I hope to be appointed as Senate Liaison to the Lobby Corps. This BCU is an incredible way to engage one-on-one with federal policymakers, and after a year of involvement, I have seen the impact it can have on our nation’s policies.
When it comes to student visas, I personally know peers who have been affected by current immigration policies and are fearful of their educational future. No one should fear for their education, especially if they are here legally on a visa. I plan to work closely with our potential international student senator, Qhawae Manala, to ensure that international students receive the most up-to-date information and support from the university. The federal administration is clearly targeting students; seven international students from UCSB were deported this year alone. To be honest, I don’t know why they were deported, and I don’t think the UC system does either— that’s a problem.
As a senator, I would like to provide workshops and resources to help international students ensure their documents are up-to-date and compliant with federal guidelines. Having worked in the EVPSA’s office this year, I’ve learned that A.S. has limited formal power when it comes to challenging federal policy. But we can take preventative action – ensuring students know their rights, have proper documentation, and feel safe. Not one Gaucho should have to live in fear.
Q17: Our campus climate is one of the best in the nation, and I take pride in that. We consistently rank among the top schools for student life. Seriously, where else in the world can you surf in the morning, head to class in the afternoon, and listen to live music in a backyard by night? I’m proud to be a Gaucho. UCSB is an incredible place, and I think most students feel that. But let’s be real –  a vast majority of students aren’t focused on campus politics. They’re worried about their next midterm, what to wear downtown on Thursday, or trying to sign a lease 16 months in advance. It’s our job in AS to make sure we’re helping students and addressing the most pressing issues on our campus, not getting caught up in performative politics. As long as AS stays grounded in serving students and meeting real needs, our campus climate will not only stay great, but it will be amazing. That’s why collaboration and communication are so important to me. If we can bring our AS offices together, streamline how we work, and stay focused on what students actually care about, we’ll see a stronger and more connected community. I also believe in revitalizing our shared spaces, updating the UCEN, restoring the koi pond, and investing in areas where students relax, recharge, and feel at home. I love this school, and I hope that shows. I want to make sure that your college experience here is not only successful, but unforgettable.

Name: Mira Than
Q1: After witnessing the frustrations of A.S. students with their system, as well as non-A.S. students towards A.S, and the difficulties of even UCSB personnel, I aim to use the Senate as a platform to remedy these issues. That being said, this idealism is not realistic, and perhaps my ideas are beyond the scope of capability, but as a governing body, the aim is always to address the needs of the community in any way possible, and to bring the standard of living for UCSB students and staff up as well. I aim to represent a constituency of those historically overlooked in the larger social scale and within this school, that being the queer, the disabled, and ethnic and gendered minorities. While I don’t believe a representative has to be part of a minority group to represent them, I am, and it gives more credence to why I want to make reforms that would provide support to said groups.
Q2: As a transfer student, I have yet to be able to be heavily involved in the UCSB community, but I am no stranger to politics and bureaucracy. I have worked in my home county on expanding a mental health program that sends trained mental health responders to concerned calls regarding problems that really shouldn't concern armed forces (known as the police). Developed by those who had lost loved ones to trigger-happy police, we demanded reforms and the expansion of the program, emphasizing a non-law enforcement line in which people can call without the fear that an erratic loved one will be shot and killed. I’ve worked with local governments for over two years at this point, and I believe those experiences of grass roots community organizing have prepared me to work in AS Senate.
Q3:
1. I wish to develop mental health resources that can be accessible without working through a phone tree with disinterested hotline workers, navigating a website, and most importantly, doesn't demand a person needs to be in a crisis to call. We should not have people be at the end of the rope to allow them access to help. I've heard a stream of complaints detailing the slowness of CAPS and unavailability of mental health resources, and this is most likely due to staff and services being underfunded, understaffed, and underpaid. I would like to work with the behavioral health services to find the root of inaccessibility to develop a resolution that would relieve these issues.

2. The main reason I am running in the first place is the inaccessibility of funds. A.S. has so much funding that no one can touch because it expects the student to carry the burden of paying for projects that can cost hundreds to thousands of dollars until they can get reimbursed, often times several months later. We are suppressing the ability to hold huge events for students with this slow, convoluted system. And A.S. students are frustrated, tired, and need a better system to serve the student body.

3.Tentatively, I would like to propose a bill to develop a storage system/space for students and staff to place items for clubs or other school-related activities, perhaps even furthering to small personal storage if viable. There are a myriad of problems that have to be, such as monitoring and having to hire man power to clean storages that aren't cleared for the summer, but I believe it would help a lot of students and staff to have a storage space on-campus.
Q4: My platform is based off the idea of civil servitude—a concept that many bureaucrats, regardless of what level they are, tend to forget. This is not a self-serving role. It’s an act of servitude and representation. All goals, especially in government, require organizing, compromise, and a sense of ambition to achieve. There's a complacency epidemic spreading through our generation, often stemming from the belief that nothing we do will create change. The biggest obstacle for both me and the student body is rejecting complacency and simply 'being okay' with the way things are. Students shouldn't have to experience large inconveniences or obstacles and feel like that is a reality that can't be change.
Q5: As I stated before, I largely want to work with the behavioral health services and find a way of implementing an efficient mental-health system. Additionally, it is important to work with the many entities within A.S. that often seem to be widely decentralized and doing their own thing with little knowledge of what the main systems of government are even doing. A platform should be based on the needs of the people, which is why I wish to audit different commissions and resource centers on what they are doing, how they are serving the people they represent, and most important, what they need. Though I am running to be part of the government, I am highly critical of if said government is actually doing what they claim they are, and the impact of the things they do. Namely, I'd like to focus my work with Basic Needs Services, CODE, CAPS, and Student Affairs.
Q6: Of course, all elected officials are expected to have available office hours to meet, a rule that many people seem to shirk. As I stated in a previous question, I want to actively go to UCSB's various services, making myself available by approaching first. Larger than my own availability, there's an issue of approachability to elected officials, which is why I want to try the alternate approach of reaching out to services that students interact with directly, rather than the indirect, elusive student government that no one really knows or is interested in. Ideally, the government should have some initiative to make themselves known and available  by communicating first. Additionally, I have this special skill called 'checking my email' and 'responding to emails' that gives me  a sharp edge in making myself available.
Q7: My identity has intersectionality with many minority groups whose needs I wish to bring forward as someone who can understand the stake of said needs. Something I pride myself in is the women-dominated field of 'listening without getting defensive'. There's a lot of debating and vaguely personal attacks that seem to happen that I understand comes from a place of fighting for something one believes in, but government is about compromise. That's not a dig at the current Senators, as even our own Congress seems to have a higher level of pettiness and disrespect for their fellow Congressman (e.g. Marjorie Taylor Green making a snide comment about another Congresswoman's false eyelashes) that even college Senators don't reach. But personally, while there are some things I am inflexible about that revolve around human rights and expanded social safety nets for students, I believe myself to be flexible about other things that other people get heated about, and keep a level-headed mind in debates that may be high-tension.
Q10: I am looking to see if the chancellor will actually acknowledge and listen to protestors, especially when said protestors are underpaid staff, and show that they are not removed from the needs of the students and staff despite their high salaries and private donors.
Q11a: Predatory rent prices, rising economic instability, the inability to get a job right after graduation, all with student debt looming on top of a student, how is anyone supposed to live in those conditions, especially those who have to make the sudden change of having parent's support to being extremely independent? Just because I believe it should be tuition-free doesn't mean it's currently viable or something that can be changed immediately, but it is indeed something I believe should happen.
Q12: No. In fact, the country services are also awful, and in my opinion, borderline evil. The reality is that most mental health services are inadequate. My main problem is the idea that one HAS to be in a state of crisis to get any attention and services. I remember when I was at the brink, calling the suicide hotline in a last ditch effort, only for no one to pick up, the ai text bot mocking me with it's automated replies. Because everyone knows people who are mentally ill are really comforted by the fact that no one wants to help them until it's too late. Even better, when the police show up for a wellness check, because a bulletproof-vested gun-swinging person only looking for evidence of abuse is the perfect first responder for mental illness. There needs to be an audit as to how CAPS functions, how the staff is doing. Name: CJ Toledo
Running For: College of Letters and Science Senator
Q1:
I’m running for Senate to make sure the most vulnerable students on this campus are seen, heard, and protected. With national politics being so volatile,  protecting each other on a local level is more essential than ever. As an Indigenous, Mexican, and Muslim student, I understand what it’s like to navigate UCSB while facing multiple forms of marginalization. I’ve been organizing and involved on campus through groups like Students for Justice in Palestine, El Congreso, and MSA because I care deeply about justice, representation, and community.

I’ve witnessed students being displaced, overworked, and overlooked. The housing crisis, food insecurity, and mental health struggles are real, and so is the lack of institutional response. I’m here to change that.

If elected, I’ll advocate for lower rent prices, higher wages for student workers, improved mental health access, inclusive and culturally affirming events, and increased support for undocumented and at-risk students. I want to be a bridge between administration and the student body, especially those who’ve been left out of conversations for too long.

We deserve a campus where students can not only survive but thrive, and I’m more than ready to fight for that future.
Q2:
My time at UCSB has been defined by organizing, advocating, and uplifting student voices; especially those who are too often pushed to the margins. I’ve been deeply involved with Students for Justice in Palestine (SJP), where we’ve built coalitions and organized actions to raise awareness, build solidarity, and demand accountability from our institution. One powerful example was the recent protest we organized in support of undocumented students. This was a collaborative effort between SJP, El Congreso, and several other organizations. We mobilized our communities to stand in solidarity with our undocumented and marginalized Gauchos, to share access to mutual aid and legal resources, with the turnout proving how powerful we are when we act together.

Beyond activism, I’ve also been directly involved in UCSB governance. I’ve served as a proxy at Senate meetings, giving me firsthand experience with the processes, expectations, and responsibilities that come with this role. I know how to navigate the system, and how to push it to do better.

Earlier in my UCSB journey, I also served as RHA President of the Santa Catalina dorms. I led weekly meetings, collaborated with leaders from dorms across campus, and helped allocate funding for events and community projects that brought people together.

Through all of this, I’ve learned how to lead with both compassion and strategy, and I’m ready to bring that to the 76th Senate.
Q3:
If elected, I plan to introduce legislation that directly addresses the crises students are facing, housing, survival, and safety,  while building long-term community resilience.
First, I will introduce a Housing Justice & Affordability Bill that ensures UCSB follows through on its promise to complete the San Benito housing project, caps annual rent increases in Isla Vista to 3% or the rate of inflation (whichever is lower), and mandates full transparency in housing waitlists. It would also guarantee university-owned housing access for UCSB students regardless of their year, because housing should be a right, not a lottery.

Second, I plan to reallocate Associated Students’ discretionary funds to create an emergency support package. My bill would shift at least $125,000 toward legal aid clinics for undocumented and at-risk students, emergency grocery and hygiene kits, housing rights education, and mental health peer support. Students should not be going hungry, homeless, or unrepresented in court while A.S. pays six figures for concerts they still charge us to attend.

Third, I will push for the creation of a Campus Safety & Justice Oversight Board: a student-majority body empowered to hold UCSB and IVPD accountable for police abuse, surveillance, and misuse of authority. This board would proactively defend students, especially BIPOC, undocumented, and disabled students, and ensure that UCSB remains a bastion of safety even as the broader nation slides into authoritarianism.

Together, these proposals form a foundation for a campus where students aren’t just surviving… we’re building something better, together.
Q4:
Describe your platform and specifically how you will work to achieve your goals during your term.

My platform is built on the belief that real change comes from the ground up — not from performative leadership or resume padding. I’m running to fight for housing justice, legal protection, food and mental health access, and to make sure UCSB stands with its most vulnerable students, not against them.

But none of this can happen alone. I’ve spent my time at UCSB organizing alongside groups like Students for Justice in Palestine, El Congreso, and MSA, and I’ve seen how powerful we are when we act together. My approach in the Senate will be rooted in that same coalition-based model: listening first, amplifying community voices, and helping bring their demands into policy.

If elected, I will continue to attend club meetings, co-host listening sessions with impacted students, and push for open feedback loops on every bill I introduce. I don’t want to write legislation for people: I want to write it with them. That’s how we make sure it’s sustainable, relevant, and just.

This campaign is about more than a seat,  it’s about building a student government that actually governs in the interests of students. I’m here to make sure your voice becomes policy, your struggles are acknowledged, and your victories are celebrated. Together, we can turn that vision into reality.
Q5:
To address housing, rent hikes, and tenant protections, I will work with Isla Vista Tenants Union (IVTU), El Congreso, the Housing Justice Research Collective, and the Office of the External Vice President for Local Affairs (EVPLA). These groups are already engaging tenants, demanding rent caps, and pushing for transparency in university development projects like San Benito.

For legal support for undocumented and at-risk students, I’ll collaborate with IDEAS at UCSB, Undocumented Student Services, CARECEN, El Centro, and community legal observers through ACLU-trained allies. These partners are already trusted in our communities and know what real protection looks like.

To fight food insecurity and improve basic needs access, I’ll work with the A.S. Food Bank, the Basic Needs Committee, the Pardall Center, the Miramar Pantry, and Santa Barbara Food Not Bombs. These are the groups filling the gaps where the university has failed.

For mental health, I’ll partner with the Commission on Student Well-Being (COSWB), CAPS Peer Program, Resilience Peers, QTBIPOC healing spaces, and groups like RCSGD and EOP that already support marginalized students through culturally rooted care.

To hold police accountable and defend civil rights on campus, I will work with Students for Justice in Palestine (SJP), the Black Student Union (BSU), MCC’s Advisory Committee, CARE, the Commission on Disability Equity (CODE), Queer Commission, and Students for Sensible Drug Policy (SSDP).

Finally, to build organizing power, I’ll collaborate with CALPIRG, Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP), YDSA, and journalistic organizations like the Daily Nexus and KCSB News to help unify our voices and bring pressure where it counts.
Q6:

In person, I’ll hold weekly office hours both on campus and in Isla Vista — not in some distant AS building, but in places that are familiar and accessible, like the Arbor if weather permits, and the library if it doesn't. I’ll also regularly attend student org meetings and coalition gatherings to stay in touch with the needs of the communities I’m representing.

Remotely, I’ll run an open digital feedback form where students can submit concerns, proposals, or questions at any time. I’ll respond weekly and share updates publicly so people know what’s being done with their input. I’ll also maintain a social media presence on Instagram to report on bills I’m supporting, campus developments, and opportunities for collaboration. In addition, I will run a Zoom option for all weekly office hours. 

I don’t believe in leadership from a distance. I believe in showing up, listening first, acting collaboratively, and staying rooted in the communities that put me here. If I’m elected, students will know that they’re not just being represented, they’re being heard.
Q7:
I want to start by acknowledging that every candidate in this race brings something valuable, and I have deep respect for anyone willing to step up and serve our community. What I believe sets me apart as candidate is the heart I bring into this work, paired with the belief that we, as students, are fully capable of building a campus where everyone can thrive. 

I genuinely love this school. I love the people, the movements, the culture, and the messiness of it all. I’m a relentless optimist who believes that a better world isn’t just possible, it’s inevitable when we come together with intention and imagination. What sets me apart is how I combine vision with action. I’m constantly imagining a better world, but I’m also grounded in the organizing, policy work, and coalition-building it takes to get there.

This campaign isn’t just about me, it’s about us. It's about lifting the voices of the most vulnerable and working toward collective liberation. I want to use this role to build something joyful, equitable, and real WITH students, not solely for them.

If given the opportunity, I promise to serve with humility, consistency, and love for this community.
Q10: I’m looking for a chancellor who is accessible, kind, and genuinely student-centered. I want someone who sees students not as statistics or sources of revenue, but as the reason this campus even exists. We need a leader who shows up, listens with humility, and prioritizes transparency and compassion over profit and PR. I want a chancellor who’s present in the community: attending student events, meeting with orgs, holding regular open forums, and walking the campus, not just for photo ops, but to truly understand what students are experiencing.  In terms of collaboration, I would advocate for a recurring meeting between student leaders and the chancellor’s office: not just with Associated Students, but with representatives from activist and cultural orgs who often get left out of decision-making. I’d also push for student-led town halls where the administration listens, not lectures, and uses that feedback to shape actual policy.  I hope the new chancellor is bold enough to challenge the UC system when needed, protect undocumented and at-risk students, expand affordable housing, and invest in the mental health, food security, and joy of our campus. That includes divesting from harmful corporations, policing practices, and choosing care over control. Ultimately, I want a chancellor who helps create a UCSB where all students can thrive, not just survive.
Q11a: Yes, UCSB should be tuition-free. The 1868 Organic Act that created the UC system promised free education for all California residents, and the 1960 California Master Plan reaffirmed that vision. For over a century, UC students paid no tuition. That changed when Governor Ronald Reagan slashed public funding and introduced tuition as a weapon against student activism. Today, students face crushing debt and basic needs insecurity.  Restoring tuition-free UC isn’t radical — it’s honoring the system’s original promise and reclaiming education as a public good, not a profit center.
Q12:
No. Given the rise in mental health diagnoses — including anxiety, depression, and a litany of other conditions — the answer is no. UCSB’s current mental health infrastructure is not equipped to meet the urgency or scale of what students are going through. This crisis is even more pronounced for students whose identities are under constant attack by an increasingly hostile political environment; specifically African American students, LGBTQIA+ students, Latina/o students, immigrants, and many others from marginalized communities.

UCSB has also failed to meaningfully reckon with the loneliness epidemic. We’re told this is one of the most vibrant places to live, but each year we see students quietly suffer, and in some cases lose their lives, to suicide, overdose, or untreated mental illness. These aren’t isolated incidents; they are symptoms of a deeper failure to address root causes and provide real support.

To begin to fix this, we need more culturally competent therapists, shorter wait times, and expanded hours for crisis care. But it goes beyond staffing. We need mental health embedded into campus life: grief circles, healing spaces, peer-led workshops, and community-based care that meets students where they are. It’s about prevention, not just crisis response.

Mental health cannot be treated as an optional add-on. It is foundational to student survival, safety, and success, and it’s time UCSB’s policies and funding reflect that.
Q13:
Yes, I’m familiar with the Title IX office and its responsibility to address and prevent sexual assault and harassment. But knowing its purpose and seeing its impact are two different things, and from what I’ve seen and heard from fellow students, UCSB’s systems fall short of supporting survivors in meaningful, trauma-informed ways.

First, survivors should never be forced to share space with their abuser. The university must develop immediate and flexible options for academic accommodations, housing adjustments, and no-contact orders that center the survivor’s comfort, not the institution’s convenience.

Second, mental health services should include professionals specifically trained in supporting survivors of sexual assault and trauma. CAPS must expand its capacity and cultural competency so that survivors receive care that validates their experience and supports their healing, without retraumatizing them in the process.

Third, the process of reporting sexual assault must be made more accessible. Right now, there’s too much friction. Survivors are often discouraged by fear, confusion, or the emotional toll of navigating bureaucratic systems. UCSB must create anonymous, low-barrier reporting tools and ensure that every survivor knows their rights and options through outreach in dorms, classrooms, and student orgs.

Ultimately, supporting survivors means believing them, protecting them, and giving them options, not obstacles. I believe UCSB has a long way to go, but with pressure and policy, we can build a system that survivors can trust.
Q14:
As a Native American, Mexican, and Muslim student, I don’t believe UCSB is effectively serving historically underrepresented communities, at least not in ways that go beyond surface-level representation.  There are a lot of brochures and diversity statements, but they don’t mean much if students still feel isolated or unsafe, and I know I’m not alone in that.

Our Muslim community doesn’t even have a permanent place to pray on campus, despite praying five times a day. I’ve seen African American students describe how they feel invisible in classrooms. Indigenous students hear land acknowledgments while the university continues to hold sacred Chumash artifacts without full repatriation or consent.

For me, this work is personal. I want every student to feel represented, safe, and truly at home here. That means involving Chumash elders in real university decisions, committing to DEI programs even under federal pressure, and shifting the curriculum so it stops centering whiteness as the default. It means listening — really listening — to the people most impacted, and turning their concerns into action.

If I’m elected, I will fight to make UCSB a place where every student can feel like they belong. Representation matters, but we also deserve power, safety, and joy. I’m committed to doing my part to make that real.

Q16:

 I’m here to build real protections, legal support, and crisis infrastructure to ensure UCSB remains a sanctuary for learning, growth, and collective safety.
Q17:

We may have different approaches or priorities, but at our core, many of us are fighting for similar values: justice, safety, access, and care.

My approach in A.S. will be to build bridges, not echo chambers. In practice, that looks like co-authoring legislation with other senators, consulting student orgs and marginalized communities before proposing bills, and prioritizing open communication. I want to help create a culture in A.S. where it’s not just about who “wins” or gets credit, but rather it’s about how we collectively make change that matters.

Outside of A.S., I’ll use my role to support grassroots organizing, connect student government to student movements, and push for a campus climate rooted in mutual respect and collective care.

Wait times remain long, short-term care is still the default, and students are often left unclear about what kind of services they can expect.
As a senator, I would push to strengthen and expand existing services. That includes deepening our partnerships with off-campus providers and making long-term therapy more financially accessible for students not covered by UC SHIP. I would also advocate for trauma-informed care training for all CAPS staff and call for more intentional hiring of clinicians who are multilingual, BIPOC, LGBTQ+, and experienced in working with underserved communities.
One major area that remains underdeveloped is transparency. Students deserve to know how long they’ll wait, who they’ll see, and what care is available to them. I would support the development of a real-time dashboard that lists provider availability, estimated wait times, and drop-in hours. I also support the creation of a student-led Mental Health Advisory Board to offer feedback and help guide CAPS’ development in ways that reflect real student needs.
Mental health services should not be designed around institutional limits — they should reflect the complexity and urgency of student wellbeing.
Q13:
Yes, I am familiar with the university’s Title IX office and its role in addressing gender-based discrimination, sexual harassment, and sexual violence on campus. The office is responsible for investigating reports, offering accommodations to survivors, and ensuring compliance with federal law. While these functions are important, many students — particularly survivors — feel that the system is bureaucratic, intimidating, and more protective of institutional liability than student wellbeing.
To better support survivors, UCSB must first center care over compliance. This means making the reporting process trauma-informed, flexible, and survivor-led. Many students avoid Title IX altogether because they fear retaliation, do not want to pursue formal investigations, or do not feel emotionally ready. I hope to collaborate with Students for Sexual and Reproductive Justice (SRJ) to push for trauma-informed reforms to the Title IX process and expand non-carceral pathways to support, including restorative justice models, survivor-led healing spaces, and expanded access to confidential advocates.
I would also work with SRJ to launch peer education campaigns that clarify what Title IX offers, what rights students have, and what alternatives exist for those who do not feel safe navigating formal systems. We need multilingual, peer-led outreach and materials that explain options clearly, without relying on legal jargon buried in policy documents.
UCSB must increase investments in prevention. This includes consent education, bystander intervention training, and support for cultural orgs and peer educators already doing this work. Support for survivors cannot begin after harm occurs. It must be proactive, community-rooted, and reflective of the complexity of survivors’ needs.
Q14:
No, I do not believe UCSB is effectively serving historically underrepresented groups. While the university often promotes diversity in its messaging, that rhetoric does not always translate into tangible support or meaningful inclusion. Many Black, Latin American, Indigenous, and LGBTQ+ students experience a campus environment that feels isolating, bureaucratic, or unresponsive, particularly when navigating housing, healthcare, mental health services, or financial aid.
One of the major issues is that support systems are often neither proactive nor culturally responsive. Resources can be difficult to find, are sometimes delivered by staff who lack cultural competency, and are frequently offered only after harm has occurred. There is also a lack of representation among staff and faculty, and the burden of advocacy too often falls on students who are already carrying the weight of systemic inequities.
At the same time, UCSB is home to powerful student organizations and cultural spaces that have supported historically marginalized communities for years. Groups such as El Congreso, BSU, QComm, and others offer community, healing, and political education, often without sufficient institutional support. Rather than highlighting these efforts only during heritage months or crisis moments, UCSB should prioritize sustained funding and meaningful collaboration with these groups.
As a student senator, I would fight for direct investment in culturally specific resources, intentional hiring practices that reflect the student body, and structural changes that make the university more accessible and responsive. Serving underrepresented communities requires more than acknowledgement. It requires redistribution, repair, and long-term commitment.
Q15:
I agree that A.S. often feels inaccessible, not because students don’t care, but because the structure, language, and visibility of A.S. are hard to navigate if you’re not already in the loop. A.S. often functions in a silo, built around jargon, formality, and insider culture. 
If we want students to be engaged, we need to give them a reason and a way to engage on their own terms. That means proving that their feedback actually shapes policy, and that their concerns are not just heard, but acted on. Engagement is earned. 
It shouldn’t be a requirement for students to sit through weekly Senate meetings that span three to even six or more hours just to stay informed. This expectation excludes students who work, care for family, or simply don’t have the time or bandwidth to parse legislative procedures. As senator, I would push for concise, plain-language summaries of major decisions, made available through org spaces, community centers, and student media (shamelessly plugging World News 4 Dummies!!).
As senator, I would use my social media as a transparent, accessible tool to share what I’m working on and how students can weigh in, whether that’s through quick polls, question boxes, or comment sections. I want students to be able to engage in small but meaningful ways, without having to make a major time commitment — unless they want to. I’ll also create clear, visual updates and host casual check-ins, so people know how their voices are being translated into action.
Involvement doesn’t have to mean showing up to every meeting. It can mean speaking up once, making a suggestion, or just staying in the loop. My goal is to make that easy — not harder.
Q16:
The threats facing international students are not hypothetical; they are real and deeply unsettling. From visa restrictions to political scapegoating, these policies create a constant sense of precarity for students who deserve safety, dignity, and full inclusion in campus life. These policies are not just discriminatory — they are dehumanizing. As someone who values historical context and believes deeply in student rights, I see this moment as part of a long pattern of using immigration status, identity, and activism as tools for social control.
This issue is deeply personal to me. The international student community at UCSB has been one of the most welcoming, genuine, and authentic groups I have encountered. My experience here would not have been the same without them. They have made UCSB feel more vibrant, more connected, and more human. I am beyond grateful for their presence and am exceptionally committed to protecting their rights to study, live, and thrive here.
As a senator, I would advocate for stronger protections for international students, both through policy and visibility. That means working with groups like the International Student Advisory Board and UCSB’s Office of International Students and Scholars to identify where gaps exist — whether in access to legal aid, emergency housing, or mental health care. I would also push for clearer campus-wide communication about students’ rights in the face of federal overreach, including language-accessible “Know Your Rights” materials and legal resource guides.
I am also deeply concerned about how political repression, including attempts to criminalize protest or silence students based on speech or national origin, affects our campus climate. I would support resolutions that affirm students’ right to peaceful expression and create support systems for those facing political intimidation, no matter who they are or what their beliefs may be. I plan to show up not only with policy, but with public solidarity.
Q17:
I believe that collaboration grounded in empathy is one of the most powerful tools we have. I want to work with others not just on the basis of shared views, but across differences because growth happens when we are willing to listen, learn, and build alongside those who challenge us. A strong A.S. is not built on agreement alone, but on mutual respect, curiosity, and the shared goal of making UCSB a more welcoming and equitable place to be.
Within A.S., I plan to learn from my peers and their lived experiences so we can build policies that are both strong and inclusive. I want to foster a culture where we respect each other’s differences, value each other’s expertise as students, and show up with a genuine desire to uplift every community on this campus. That includes amplifying the work of boards, commissions, and student orgs, while ensuring that collaboration feels meaningful — not transactional. We must trust that we will hold each other accountable.
Outside of A.S., I want the broader campus climate to reflect the kind of care and intentionality practiced inside Senate. I’ll work with cultural orgs, peer educators, and centers like EOP and DIRC to co-create spaces of visibility, joy, and support. Campus climate changes when we build trust, listen well, and move with purpose together, not through statements alone.

Name: Qhawe Manala
Q1: I’m running for International Senator because I believe UCSB should be a place where every student, regardless of where they come from, feels seen, supported, and empowered to thrive. Beyond a rigorous academic regime, as an international, I've had to navigate financial, cultural, and emotional challenges that are all too common among foreign students. I’ve also seen how vibrant and driven this community is—and I want to ensure our voices are represented in decision-making processes. That’s why my platform is built on three pillars: Getting Represented, Getting Supported, and Getting Connected

As an aspiring athlete, I’ve learned how to lead, collaborate, and stay disciplined under pressure—skills I plan to bring to the Senate. Furthermore, I am in the latter stages of developing an app called BookSwap that facilitates the free and direct trade of textbooks amongst students, born out of the challenges many of us face with rising costs and limited resources. Before UCSB, I led a campaign that distributed over 3,000 books to 4 underprivileged schools in Johannesburg, South Africa, serving a community of approximately 5000 children. The key lesson I’ve learned from service to others is that lasting change begins with establishing organised systems at the institutional level. I see the Senate as the vehicle for systemic change.
Q3:
1. International Student Emergency Relief and Financial Inclusion Act
This bill will advocate for the expansion of emergency relief funds specifically accessible to international students, who are often excluded from state and federal aid. It will propose a collaborative funding model involving the Office of International Students & Scholars (OISS), UCSB Financial Aid, and external donors. In addition to emergency grants, the bill will push for the creation of a centralised scholarship portal for international students and support initiatives like textbook swaps to reduce academic costs. By making financial support more inclusive and accessible, this resolution aims to uplift students facing economic hardship and ensure that financial strain does not derail academic success.

2. International Housing Equity and Community Building Act
International students often face housing discrimination, visa-related limitations, and a lack of social integration. This bill will advocate for a designated quota of university housing beds reserved for international students, early access to housing applications, and culturally responsive support through OISS and Housing & Residential Services. It will also push for the creation of more socially engaging housing environments in the first-year experience, particularly in the first quarter, to reduce isolation. Additionally, the resolution will mandate an annual review of international student housing satisfaction and ensure housing policies are equitable, inclusive, and informed by student feedback.

3. Global Voices Forum and Professional Empowerment Resolution
International students often lack access to professional growth opportunities due to visa restrictions and limited networking support. This resolution will propose the creation of a Global Voices Forum—an official council composed of international student leaders across campus organisations, working in tandem with A.S. to share updates, represent student needs, and contribute to international student policy. The bill will also advocate for increased on-campus job and internship opportunities tailored for F-1 visa compliance, professional networking events, and mentorship programs in collaboration with Career Services. Together, this builds both representation and tangible pathways to success.

To strengthen support, I’ll fight for expanded emergency relief funding, housing access, and textbook affordability through bills that target financial and academic barriers.

To foster connection, I’ll advocate for community-focused housing, culturally inclusive events, and more F-1 friendly job and networking opportunities.
Q5: I’m committed to turning these ideas into action by working closely with OISS, Housing, and Career Services. Let’s get represented. Let’s get supported. Let’s get connected.
Q6: Accessibility is key to effective leadership, and I’m committed to making sure international students—and all students—can easily reach me throughout my term. In person, I plan to hold regular office hours on campus and attend international student events to stay engaged with the community. I’ll also use polls, Q&As, and DMs to hear directly from students and address concerns quickly. Follow me on IG @qmanala_for_senate
Q7: I bring a unique perspective as a South African international student, student-athlete, and campus leader who understands the challenges of adapting, connecting, and thriving at UCSB. I’ve led initiatives that impacted thousands back home and I’m ready to do the same here—by turning ideas into action and delivering real results. I’m not just running to represent international students—I’m running to empower them.

As International Senator, I plan to work with the chancellor by representing student voices in administrative discussions and ensuring that international concerns are part of their strategic vision. Q12:

Q13:
Yes, UCSB has established structures to address sexual assault and harassment, primarily through its Title IX office, which handles reports and ensures compliance with federal regulations. By continuing to build upon these systems, UCSB can create a safer, more supportive environment for all students.
